In recent years, mobile health and fitness applications have become widely used tools for supporting personal training, nutrition management, physical progress tracking, and lifestyle improvement. These applications are used by beginners, regular gym members, athletes, and individuals seeking healthier daily habits. The fitness domain is strongly connected to several factors such as workout planning, meal organization, injury prevention, body transformation, motivation, and long-term consistency. As a result, there is a growing need for intelligent digital systems capable of guiding users according to their personal goals, physical condition, nutrition preferences, and progress over time.

However, many existing fitness applications still provide general workout routines and standard meal plans that are not sufficiently adapted to each user. A user who wants to lose weight, gain muscle, recover from an injury, train at home, or prepare for a competition may receive recommendations that do not fully match his or her actual situation. In addition, users often struggle to maintain motivation because progress tracking, social interaction, challenges, rewards, and feedback are separated across different applications or are not deeply integrated into the fitness experience.

Another important issue is safety and reliability. A workout plan that ignores injuries or physical limitations may increase the risk of incorrect training, while a nutrition plan that ignores allergies, food preferences, or expert validation may be unsuitable for the user. Exercise execution is also a common problem, since users may perform movements incorrectly without receiving form feedback. These limitations show the need for a more complete fitness platform that combines personalization, artificial intelligence, expert approval, progress analysis, and user engagement features.

Therefore, this project focuses on the development of an AI-powered mobile fitness application that supports users through personalized workout generation, smart nutrition planning, exercise form analysis,

recovery guidance, community interaction, challenges, achievements, and rewards. The project is motivated by the need to provide a more adaptive, safe, and engaging fitness experience within a single integrated system.

The main problem addressed in this project is the lack of a complete and personalized fitness application that can adapt workout plans, nutrition recommendations, progress tracking, and user engagement features to the real needs of each user. Many users require guidance that considers their fitness goal, physical profile, training location, injury status, food preferences, allergies, available ingredients, and progress history, but existing solutions often treat these elements separately or provide generic recommendations.

The objective of this project is to design and implement an AI-powered mobile fitness system that generates personalized workout and nutrition plans, supports safe exercise execution, predicts user progress, and improves motivation through social and gamification features. At the first level, the mobile application represents the direct interaction point with the user. The mobile application does not directly access the database or AI models. Instead, it communicates with the backend through HTTP API requests.

At the second level, the backend layer acts as the central controller of the system. It was developed using PHP and organized through a centralized API router. The backend receives requests from the mobile application, verifies authentication, processes user actions, communicates with the database, and calls the appropriate service when needed. AI module. When a user requests a nutrition plan, the backend sends calorie needs, preferences, allergies, fridge ingredients, and expert approval data to
AI. The backend therefore works as the bridge between the mobile interface, the database, and the AI modules.

Dividing the system into blocks makes the architecture easier to understand, implement, test, and maintain.
The main design blocks of the proposed system are described in the following subsections.

The mobile application block represents the user-facing part of the system. It was developed using React Native and Expo, which allowed the creation of a mobile interface suitable for Android testing. This block contains all the screens and navigation flows used by the user, including authentication, onboarding, dashboard, workout plan, workout player, nutrition plan, smart meal assistant, progress tracking, community, messages, challenges, rewards, achievements, profile, notifications, recovery, and competition preparation.

The main role of this block is to collect user inputs and display personalized results. analysis, log water intake, update weight, join challenges, redeem rewards, send messages, and interact with community posts. Therefore, this block is not only responsible for display, but also for continuous interaction between the user and the system.

The backend API block acts as the central communication layer of the system. It was developed using PHP and exposes several endpoints through a centralized API router. The mobile application does not communicate directly with the database or the AI files; instead, all requests pass through the backend API.

For example, when a user logs in, the backend verifies the credentials and returns an authentication token. Services handle more specialized logic such as workout AI generation, nutrition AI generation, progress, goal suggestion, and AI chat communication. In this project, the communication architecture follows a client-server model, where the React Native mobile application acts as the client and the PHP backend acts as the server. The mobile application never accesses the database or AI model files directly; all communication passes through the API layer.

The mobile application communicates with the backend through HTTP requests using the API service implemented in the frontend. The API base URL points to the local backend server running on the development machine. Each backend operation is exposed as an endpoint, such as
. These endpoints are routed through a centralized PHP router, which identifies the requested endpoint and dispatches it to the correct controller method.

Most frontend-backend exchanges use JSON format. For example, when the user updates the profile, the mobile app sends a JSON payload containing fields such as weight, height, goal, activity level, training location, injuries, allergies, and food preferences. When the backend responds, it also returns JSON data containing status codes, messages, user profiles, workout plans, nutrition plans, progress statistics, AI predictions, social posts, challenge data, or reward information. This structured format allows the frontend to parse responses easily and update the correct screen state.

Authentication communication is handled using bearer tokens. After login or registration, the backend returns a token to the mobile application. This token is stored on the client side and attached to protected API requests in the

header. On the backend, protected routes call the authentication middleware to verify the token before allowing access to private data such as profile information, messages, progress logs, workouts, nutrition plans, and rewards.

Database communication is handled on the backend using PHP Data Objects. PDO was used to execute prepared SQL queries, which improves security and reduces the risk of SQL injection. The backend uses these queries to create, read, update, and delete records in MySQL tables such as users, user profiles, workouts, nutrition plans, progress, friends, messages, posts, clubs, challenges, rewards, redemptions, achievements, notifications, recovery plans, competition plans, meal reviews, and exercise tutorial reviews.
Communication with the local AI modules is performed through backend service classes. For workout generation, the backend service sends the user profile to the Python
AI module and receives a structured workout plan. For nutrition generation, the backend sends calorie targets, preferences, allergies, fridge ingredients, and expert approval data to

AI. Because nutrition payloads can be large, the backend writes the data to temporary JSON files and passes the file path to the Python script. This avoids command-line size limitations and makes the AI call more reliable
AI receives uploaded video files and returns JSON analysis results.

For video communication, the mobile application uses multipart form-data instead of normal JSON. The request contains the video file, exercise name, and optional target repetition count. The backend validates the upload, stores the file temporarily, calls the local Python video analyzer, and returns the output to the mobile application. The returned result includes analyzed duration, repetition count, form score, confidence level, detected mistakes, and feedback messages.

During development and testing, the backend was hosted locally on the development computer using PHP’s built-in server, while the mobile application communicated with it through the local network IP address and port. This required the smartphone and computer to be connected to the same network. Correct IP configuration was necessary because any change in the local address could break the connection between the mobile client and backend API.

This communication block is therefore responsible for connecting all parts of the system. It ensures that user inputs reach the backend, database records are retrieved and updated correctly, AI modules receive the required data, and the mobile application receives usable results. By using HTTP, JSON, bearer authentication, prepared SQL queries, multipart upload, and structured AI responses, the system maintains a clear and organized communication flow between all components.

Many users want personalized workout and nutrition support, but not everyone has access to a personal coach, a nutrition expert, or a structured training environment. One limitation of the project is that the prototype was tested mainly in a local development environment and not with a large number of real users over a long period. Therefore, the system should be considered a functional prototype that can be improved further before real public deployment.

Overall, the project achieved its main objective: developing a complete AI-supported fitness mobile application that combines personalization, tracking, expert validation, video analysis, social motivation, and gamification. The result is a practical prototype that demonstrates how local AI modules can be integrated into a mobile health and fitness system in a useful and responsible way.

Although the proposed system achieved its main objectives, several improvements can be considered in future work. The first important improvement would be to test the application with a larger number of real users. Long-term user testing would make it possible to evaluate how effective the workout plans, nutrition recommendations, progress tracking, and motivational features are over several weeks or months.
Another possible improvement is to expand the datasets used by the artificial intelligence modules.
AI could be trained with a larger exercise dataset containing more movements, equipment types, difficulty levels, injury constraints, and expert-labeled suitability scores.

AI could also be improved with more diverse meal datasets, including regional foods, cultural preferences, prices, preparation time, and ingredient availability. This would make the recommendations more realistic for different users and locations.

AI module could also be extended. In the current version, video analysis depends on camera angle, lighting, body visibility, and supported exercise templates. Future versions could support more exercises, provide more detailed biomechanical feedback, compare user movement with expert demonstrations, and improve accuracy under different recording conditions. Real-time camera analysis could also be added instead of relying only on uploaded or recorded videos.

From a security and deployment perspective, the system could be improved by moving from a local development setup to a secure production environment. This would require HTTPS, stronger password management, email verification, password reset, role-based access control, server monitoring, backup strategies, and better protection of personal health data. Since the application handles sensitive user information, privacy and data protection must remain a priority.

The expert review system can also be developed further. In future work, certified coaches and nutritionists could have dedicated dashboards to review meals, exercises, user progress, and AI recommendations. This would create a stronger human-in-the-loop system where AI assists experts instead of replacing them.

Finally, the application could be extended with wearable device integration, multilingual support, personalized notifications, advanced analytics, gym partnership features, and more realistic reward systems. These improvements would make the system more scalable, more useful, and more suitable for real-world use.

In conclusion, the project opens the way for a larger digital fitness platform that combines artificial intelligence, expert supervision, and community motivation. Future work should focus on real-user validation, stronger datasets, improved AI accuracy, production security, and deeper collaboration with fitness and nutrition professionals.
